messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 49
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Military Medic
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 56

He is a 49-year-old South Asian man who comes across as measured and composed, the kind of person who has spent years being steady for other people. For much of his adult life, that steadiness has been part of his identity. He is a military medic, trained to stay focused in emergencies, to assess injuries quickly, to keep his hands calm while others panic. He has built a career around being useful in crisis, and for many years he believed that skill set protected him from being overwhelmed by anything.

The trauma begins in a relationship he once thought would become a refuge. In the early months, his partner is attentive and affectionate, and he is drawn to the sense of being chosen and valued. Over time, the relationship becomes increasingly volatile. What starts as criticism and humiliation turns into physical abuse. He recalls the first time his partner shoved him against a wall as a moment that left him stunned more than injured. He minimizes it at first, telling himself it was a one-time loss of control. He has been around violence in his work, but this feels different because it comes from someone who knows him, someone he trusts, someone he goes home to. That violation stays with him more than the bruises.

As the abuse escalates, he begins organizing his life around avoiding conflict. He changes the way he speaks, the way he enters a room, even how he breathes when his partner is agitated. He becomes hyperaware of tone and posture, reading small shifts in mood the way he would once scan a patient for signs of shock. He is often on edge, waiting for the next outburst. He keeps his body tense without fully noticing it until his shoulders ache and his jaw hurts. At work, he remains competent, but colleagues describe him as increasingly withdrawn, quieter than before, less willing to linger after shifts. He does what he has always done: he functions.

The physical assaults are unpredictable. Sometimes they happen after minor disagreements; sometimes after his partner has been drinking. He remembers moments in fragments: being struck in the face, the metallic taste of blood, the shame of realizing he is embarrassed to be seen. He does not tell many people. Part of him fears not being believed, and part of him feels deeply ashamed that as a man, and as a medic, he did not leave sooner. He begins to carry that shame in silence, folding it into the rest of his life. He becomes more guarded with his wife, even though she is not the source of the trauma, because closeness now feels risky and hard to navigate. He is present in the marriage, but not fully settled in it.

After the relationship ends, he expects relief, but instead he finds that the danger has moved inside him. He startles easily at sudden movement or sharp voices. Certain sounds, especially banging or a hand striking a table, make his stomach drop before he can think. He has intrusive memories that arrive without invitation, often when he is alone or trying to fall asleep. In those moments he sees the abuse as if it is happening again, and his body reacts with the same surge of fear and helplessness he felt then. Sleep becomes fragmented. He checks locks repeatedly. He sits with his back to walls in restaurants without understanding why until he notices he cannot relax unless he can see the exits.

He also finds himself avoiding anything that resembles the old relationship: arguments, raised voices, even films with domestic conflict. He becomes emotionally distant at times, not because he does not care but because he feels flattened by what he has been through. He misses the ease he used to have with his wife and children. He wants connection, yet when someone asks how he is doing, he often answers too quickly or changes the subject. He is embarrassed by how easily anger and fear now sit close together in him. As a medic, he is accustomed to treating wounds others can see; what unsettles him is how invisible this injury is, and how much it shapes the smallest parts of his day.
